cells.tense: You are here with the weight of knowing what to do and the standing to do it.
cells.act: tend the small thing and learn from it
cells.ask: Tend one real thing that's already yours — a plant, a machine, a corner of the room — without fixing anything, watching what it asks for rather than what you'd plan.
cells.core:
You're standing at the point where what matters shows itself before the reason does, and that showing-up is doing its job in the work you've got. What's finished, you put down cleanly — no drag, no second-guessing — and that's why your hands are free for what comes next. It isn't a conclusion you reached; it arrives before the argument does.

What holds this steady is treating the thing you look after as something with its own way of growing, not a project to finish. So keep it small and keep it true: tend one real thing that's yours, without correcting anything — no fixes, no improvements, just fresh attention to what it's actually asking for. What you learn comes back with you and steadies what you already trust.

cells.tense: You will have settled the not-yet question before the day arrives that could answer it.
cells.act: write the facts down in order, without feeling words
cells.ask: When the next worry about what's coming pulls, write out only what is actually on record — dates, decisions, what has happened — and stop at the last true line.
cells.core:
You're bracing against a future that can't be written in yet, and the bracing is doing the writing. Where you know what matters early, that becomes a standing to resolve things ahead of time, because getting there first feels like the safe place. But the clean release you carry — the kind that comes as fulfilment, not defeat — only arrives after something is finished, and nothing here is finished yet. So the pushing has nowhere to land, and your body carries the difference.

You don't have to solve the future to stop bracing. When the next worry pulls, write out only what is actually on record — the dates, the decisions, what has happened — and stop at the last true line. The page holds what's real; the rest can wait for the day it becomes real.

cells.tense: You were released once, cleanly, and you have been standing at that closed door since.
cells.act: lay the one step you can see, solidly
cells.ask: Lay just the next step you can actually see — a repair, a form, a drawer sorted — and stop once it stands, not when it's perfect.
cells.core:
You stood at a door after it closed, and the standing used up the room. The sense of what matters is still there in you, but it's drawing on nothing — the release happened and you didn't come through into the next thing. So the middle of you is running on empty: not blind, just starved. What should have been fulfilment reads as something you're still atoning for, and your hands stay still.

You don't fix this by forcing feeling into the tired place. Give the body something solid to stand on and direction comes back through the hands. Lay just the next step you can actually see — a repair, a form, a drawer sorted — and stop once it stands, not when it's perfect. What's solid under your feet holds the rest.

cells.tense: You are already writing this, and the room you're writing in has your hand down.
cells.act: care for it with fresh hands and see what it needs
cells.ask: Pick up care of something alive or working that you keep going, and for a week notice what it wants without filing it as upkeep.
cells.core:
There's a way you handle things — you let go at the right moment, you know what deserves your hand — and it's doing its work quietly through you, without your name on it. Asked, you'd say the situation sorted itself out, or that anyone would have done the same. The hand is real; it just isn't owned. So what shows up is knowing what matters and calling it common sense, which is how a gift gets kept small.

Go back to the simpler form. Pick up care of something alive or working that you keep going, and for a week notice what it wants without filing it as upkeep. One living thing, watched plainly. No speech about it. Notice your own hand in it, and count that.

A reader could reasonably say 'I'm not commanding anything, I'm just getting through the week.' The ask survives being wrong because it teaches the person something usable regardless — tending one real thing and learning from it works even if the reading misnames what's happening. The sentence that serves the writer is the one that admires the mastery: 'directing the fire with full knowledge of its cost' — it sounds deep and says nothing the person can check.
